title: Predict the output: concat without reassignment
shortTitle: Predict the output: concat without reassignment
keyPoints: String is immutable – concat() returns a NEW String, does not modify the original
If you do not assign the result, the original is unchanged
s.concat("World") without s = s.concat("World") has no visible effect
This is one of the most common interview trick questions
Understanding this concept is essential for Java interviews at senior level

s1_definition.oneliner: concat() returns a new String. Without reassignment, the original is unchanged. Output: "Hello" (not "HelloWorld").
s1_definition.profdef:
The trick:

- `s.concat("World")` creates a new String "HelloWorld" but does NOT assign it to `s`.
- `s` still points to the original "Hello".
- The new String is garbage-collected immediately.
s1_definition.analogy: Asking the printer to create a new document (concat) but never picking it up (no assignment). The original document on your desk is unchanged.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  s = "Hello"
  s.concat(" World") → creates new String "Hello World" → NOT assigned → garbage
  s is still "Hello"
  Output: Hello
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
String.concat() returns a new String without modifying the original. Without reassignment, the original is unchanged. This is because String is immutable.

One sentence to remember: String methods return new Strings – without reassignment, the original never changes.
